takeaways: Every chip is tested because the fab makes defects; yield and fault coverage together set how many bad chips still ship, DL = 1 − Y<sup>(1 − T)</sup>.
Fault models turn countless physical defects into a short logical list: stuck-at for static logic, transition and path delay for timing.
Collapsing (equivalence, dominance, checkpoints) shrinks the list before ATPG; fault simulation with dropping measures coverage vector by vector.
The D-algorithm activates a fault, propagates D or D̄ to an output, and justifies every value back to the primary inputs.
Full scan turns a sequential chip into combinational logic for ATPG, at the cost of a multiplexer per flip-flop and (N + 1)P + N shift clocks.
Boundary scan tests board wiring through four pins; in a daisy chain the register lengths add, and TMS walks every chip through the same 16 states.
BIST puts an LFSR and a MISR on the chip; maximal-length LFSRs give 2ⁿ − 1 vectors and an n-bit MISR aliases with probability about 2⁻ⁿ.
Memories need march tests; March C− (10n) catches stuck-at, transition, address and unlinked coupling faults, and memory BIST runs it on chip.
Test is spread over wafer, package, board and system; SoC cores are reached through wrappers and a TAM, scheduled within pins and power.
Analog blocks are tested against specifications: DNL, INL, offset, gain, SNR, SINAD and ENOB, with structural checks such as IDDQ and loopback.

bank.q: Explain why every fabricated chip is tested, and how yield and fault coverage decide the quality the customer receives. Use a yield of 0.80 to show the effect of coverage.
outline: Defects come from the fab; verification cannot find them
Where test sits from wafer to customer
Yield and its link to die area
Defect level DL = 1 − Y^(1 − T) with numbers
answer: Why test at all. Fabrication adds random defects: dust that breaks a wire, a missing contact, a pinhole in the gate oxide. Verification only proves the design is right; it cannot see whether one particular copy was built right. So every die is driven with known inputs and its outputs are compared with the expected ones.

Where test happens. Wafer probe removes bad die before packaging money is spent; final test removes parts damaged in assembly or too slow at temperature; burn-in removes weak parts; board and system tests catch what is left. Each later step costs more per failure.

Yield. Yield Y is the fraction of die that are good. Random defects make it fall with die area A and defect density D, roughly Y = e−A·D; a 1 cm² die at 0.2 killer defects per cm² gives Y = e−0.2 = 0.82.

Fault coverage. Fault coverage T is the fraction of modelled faults (for example single stuck-at faults) that the test vectors detect, measured by fault simulation. It describes the test program, not the fab.

answer: Reading the table. Four more points of coverage cut the escapes about five times, from 11,095 to 2,229 parts per million. Because coverage sits in the exponent, the last few per cent matter most, and that is where test engineering effort goes.

Cost. Test is paid per second of tester time: cost per die = (R × t) ÷ s for a tester rate R, test time t and s sites tested together. Higher coverage means more vectors and longer t, so the team balances test cost against the cost of escapes: field returns, warranty and lost customers.

bank.q: Define defect, fault, error and failure with an example of each. Explain why fault models are needed, using the single stuck-at faults of a two-input NAND gate.
outline: Why defects cannot be targeted directly
Single stuck-at model and fault count 2L
answer: Defect. A physical flaw in the manufactured chip. Example: a dust particle breaks a metal wire.
Fault. The logical model of a defect, used by test software. Example: the broken wire behaves as a line stuck at 0.
Error. A wrong value on a line at some moment, caused by the fault when the circuit is exercised. Example: an adder output is 0110 instead of 0111.
Failure. Lost function: the error reaches an output and the chip misses its specification. Example: a phone screen stays black.

Why models are needed. Defects come in endless sizes, shapes and places, so no program can list them. A fault model maps them onto a finite logical list that a program can enumerate, generate tests for and count; fault coverage is defined on that list.

answer: Collapsing. A/0, B/0 and Z/1 give identical tables, so they are equivalent: 4 classes remain. Z/0 is detected by every test of A/1, so it dominates A/1 and can be dropped: 3 faults remain, and {01, 10, 11} is a complete test set of three vectors.

Other models. Bridging faults (two lines shorted, wired-AND or wired-OR), transistor stuck-open (needs a two-vector test), and transition or path delay faults (need launch and capture at speed) cover defects the stuck-at model misses.

bank.q: Explain scan design with a neat diagram of a scan chain. Define full scan, partial scan, controllability and observability, and give the test procedure and its cost.
outline: Why sequential circuits are hard: controllability and observability
Muxed-D scan cell, SE and SI
Scan chain and the three phases
Cost: area, delay, pins, test time (N + 1)P + N
answer: The problem. A sequential circuit hides its state. Controllability is how easily a node can be set to 0 or 1 from the primary inputs; observability is how easily its value can be seen at a primary output. Deep state makes both poor, so a fault may need a long input sequence to excite and another to observe, and ATPG time explodes.
The scan cell. A 2:1 multiplexer in front of each D flip-flop chooses the functional input D when scan enable SE = 0, and the scan input SI when SE = 1.

answer.text: The chain. Joining Q of each cell to SI of the next forms a shift register from the scan-in pin to the scan-out pin. The example chain below has three cells and a small logic block.

answer: Procedure. (1) Shift in: SE = 1, the pattern enters one bit per clock, the bit for the last cell first. (2) Capture: SE = 0 for one clock; every flip-flop loads the logic's response. (3) Shift out: SE = 1, the response leaves through scan-out while the next pattern enters.
Trace. In the figure, loading 011 (SI = 1, 1, 0) and capturing gives 111 in a good chip; with D1 stuck-at-0 the chip captures 011, and the third bit out is 0 instead of 1.

Full scan makes every flip-flop a scan cell, so ATPG sees only combinational logic between pseudo-primary inputs and outputs: high coverage, simple ATPG. Partial scan converts only the flip-flops that break feedback loops: less area and delay, but ATPG must handle the remaining sequential logic.

Cost. One multiplexer per flip-flop (area), one multiplexer delay on each functional path, the SE net and two or more pins, and test time. With overlapped shifting, P patterns on a chain of N cells take (N + 1) × P + N clocks; 1000 patterns on one 200-cell chain take 201,200 clocks, on four 50-cell chains 51,050.
Check. The three-cell trace uses (3 + 1) × 1 + 3 = 7 clocks: three to shift in, one to capture, three to shift out, matching the formula.

bank.q: Describe boundary scan with the architecture of an IEEE 1149.1 device and the TAP controller state diagram. Explain how the instructions select the registers.
outline: TAP pins: TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO, optional TRST
Boundary cells at each digital pin, BSR
answer: Aim. Boundary scan tests the wiring between chips on a board, where fine-pitch and ball-grid-array parts leave no probe points, through four pins on each chip.

Pins. TCK clocks the logic; TMS steers the TAP controller; TDI and TDO carry serial data in and out. TMS and TDI are sampled on the rising edge of TCK and TDO changes on the falling edge. TRST is an optional asynchronous reset.

Boundary cells. A cell sits between the core and every digital signal pad. In normal mode it passes the signal; in test mode an output cell can drive the pad from a stored bit and an input cell can capture the pad value. All cells form the boundary-scan register (BSR).

Registers. The instruction register (IR, at least 2 bits) holds the current instruction. The data registers are the 1-bit bypass register, the BSR and, on most chips, the 32-bit IDCODE register. The instruction decides which data register is connected between TDI and TDO.

answer.text: TAP controller. A 16-state machine moved by TMS on each rising TCK edge. Five TCK edges with TMS = 1 reach Test-Logic-Reset from any state. Each of the DR and IR columns has Select, Capture (parallel load), Shift (one bit per TCK), Exit1, Pause, Exit2 and Update (copy to the outputs).

bank.q: Explain the BIST architecture with a pattern generator and a response analyser. Work out the states of a 4-bit LFSR and the aliasing probability of a 16-bit MISR.
outline: Why BIST: tester cost, at-speed and field test
answer: Why BIST. An external tester is expensive per second and cannot always apply vectors at the chip's full speed. BIST puts the pattern generator and the response checker on the chip, so the chip can test itself at power-on, after packaging and in the field.

answer.text: Architecture. The test pattern generator (TPG) drives the circuit under test (CUT); the output response analyser (ORA) compresses the outputs into a signature; the controller resets, seeds, counts the vectors and compares the signature with the stored golden value.

answer: LFSR. A shift register whose input is the XOR of chosen taps. With taps from a primitive polynomial an n-stage LFSR visits all 2ⁿ − 1 non-zero states. The seed must be non-zero, because all zeros feeds back zero for ever.

answer.text: Worked states. 4 bits, shift left, f = b3 ⊕ b0 into b0, seed 0001:

answer: The seed returns after 15 clocks = 2⁴ − 1, so the LFSR is maximal-length.

MISR. An LFSR with an XOR at each stage input where one CUT output enters each clock. After N vectors it holds an n-bit signature. A faulty circuit can end on the golden signature (aliasing) with probability about 2⁻ⁿ: for 16 bits, 1 ÷ 65,536 = 1.53 × 10⁻⁵.
Delivery. Test-per-clock applies one vector per clock to the CUT inputs; test-per-scan shifts each vector into scan chains, N × (L + 1) clocks for N vectors and chains of L cells.

Costs and limits. Area for the LFSR, MISR and controller; a little delay where multiplexers enter functional paths; random-pattern-resistant faults that need weighting, reseeding or test points; and a golden signature that must be re-simulated whenever the design changes. A pass means the signature matched, not that the chip is perfect.
Check. All 15 listed states are different and none is 0000, as a maximal-length 4-bit LFSR requires.

bank.q: The circuit has G1 = AND(A, B), G2 = OR(G1, C) and Z = AND(G2, D). Use the D-algorithm to find a test for G1 stuck-at-0. Show the D-frontier and J-frontier at each step, and verify the test.
outline: Activate G1/0: G1 = 1, so A = B = 1
Vector ABCD = 1101; good Z = 1, faulty Z = 0
answer: Notation. D means good 1 and faulty 0; D̄ means good 0 and faulty 1. Non-controlling values: 1 for AND, 0 for OR.
Activate. The fault is G1 stuck-at-0, so the good circuit must have G1 = 1: G1 = D. An AND output of 1 needs A = 1 and B = 1, which go on the J-frontier.
Propagate through G2. G2 = OR(G1, C) is on the D-frontier. Set C = 0 (non-controlling): G2 = OR(D, 0) = D.
Propagate through Z. Z = AND(G2, D) is now on the D-frontier. Set D = 1: Z = AND(D, 1) = D, so the difference reaches the output.
Justify. A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 and D = 1 are all primary inputs, so the J-frontier empties without conflict and no backtrack is needed.
Answer. ABCD = 1101 detects G1 stuck-at-0: Z = 1 in the good circuit and 0 in the faulty one.

Why each side value matters. With C = 1 the OR gate would output 1 in both circuits and block the fault; with D = 0 the last AND would output 0 in both. ATPG chooses non-controlling values exactly to avoid this.

bank.q: Explain how a march test is applied to a memory. Run March C− on a 4-address bit-oriented memory in which a 0 → 1 write to cell 0 inverts cell 3, and show where it fails. Why does address order matter?
outline: Trace on 4 cells with the coupling fault
answer: Notation. A march element visits every address in one order (⇑ ascending, ⇓ descending, ⇕ either) and does the same operations at each. w0/w1 write 0/1; r0/r1 read and expect 0/1, and a mismatch is a fail.
March C−. ⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇑(r1, w0); ⇓(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0); ⇕(r0). Operations per address: 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10, so the length is 10n; for n = 4 that is 40 operations.

answer.text: Trace with the coupling fault (aggressor cell 0, victim cell 3, rising write of the aggressor inverts the victim):

answer: Where it fails. The read of cell 3 in the second element expects 0 but finds 1. The fault was excited at address 0 and observed three addresses later in the same ascending pass.

Why order matters. Here the aggressor is below the victim, so an ascending pass reaches the victim after the aggressor has been written. When the aggressor is above the victim (say cell 2 disturbs cell 0), the ascending pass has already read the victim; the fault is then caught by the next element's read, ⇑(r1, w0), or by a descending element. Running both orders with both transitions covers every aggressor-victim pair. On a 4-cell memory, March C− catches all 72 single coupling faults, while MATS+ (5n) misses 40.
Other faults. A cell that cannot rise (up-transition fault) fails the r1 of ⇑(r1, w0); a stuck-at cell fails one of the reads; an address that writes the wrong cell fails a later read of that cell.

Check. Total operations for the whole test on 4 cells: 10 × 4 = 40, of which the failing read is the 12th: 4 writes in the first element, then r0 and w1 at addresses 0, 1 and 2 (6 operations), then r0 at address 3.

bank.q: A board has four JTAG chips in a daisy chain with instruction registers of 4, 5, 8 and 4 bits and boundary registers of 32, 48, 120 and 16 cells. Explain how ten nets between them are tested with EXTEST, and find the TCK cycles for the test.
outline: Procedure: SAMPLE/PRELOAD, EXTEST, capture and shift
answer: Chain lengths. Instruction bits = 4 + 5 + 8 + 4 = 21. Boundary bits = 32 + 48 + 120 + 16 = 216.

Procedure. (1) Reset with TMS = 1 for five edges, then go to Run-Test/Idle. (2) Load SAMPLE/PRELOAD and shift the first drive pattern into the BSRs, so the pins start from safe values. (3) Load EXTEST: the output cells now drive the nets. (4) For each pattern, Capture-DR stores what the input cells receive, Shift-DR moves those bits out while the next drive pattern moves in, and Update-DR applies it.

answer.text: Codes for the nets. Give each net a different code, leaving out all 0s and all 1s, so a net stuck at 0 or 1 cannot look correct. Ten nets need ⌈log₂(10 + 2)⌉ = 4 bits, so 4 parallel test vectors. Vector k drives bit k of every net's code.

answer: Diagnosis. If nets 3 and 5 are shorted and the short acts as wired-AND, both receive 0011 AND 0101 = 0001, so both read 0001 instead of their codes: two wrong nets with the same received code point to a short between them. An open on net 7 leaves its receiver floating; if it reads 1111 or 0000, that code belongs to no net, which flags an open.

answer.text: TCK count. From Run-Test/Idle an IR scan takes 4 edges to reach Shift-IR, 21 shift edges and 2 to return: 27. A DR scan takes 3 + 216 + 2 = 221.
answer.pre:
reset and enter Run-Test/Idle      5 + 1 =   6
IR scan: SAMPLE/PRELOAD                    27
DR scan: preload vector 1                 221
IR scan: EXTEST                            27
DR scans: 4 × 221 (capture v1 … v4)       884
total                                   1,165 TCK

answer: Time. At a 10 MHz TCK, 1,165 × 100 ns = 116.5 µs for all ten nets.
Check. The fourth DR scan captures the response to vector 4 and shifts it out; the bits it shifts in are not used, so four DR scans after EXTEST are enough.

bank.q: A scan design has 10,000 scan cells and 8 tester scan channels. Without compression it uses 8 chains and needs 2,000 patterns; with a decompressor and compactor it uses 400 internal chains and needs 2,400 patterns. Compare shift clocks and tester data.
answer: With compression. 10,000 ÷ 400 = 25 cells per internal chain; the decompressor fills all 400 chains from the 8 channels each clock. Clocks = (25 + 1) × 2,400 + 25 = 62,400 + 25 = 62,425.
Time ratio. 2,503,250 ÷ 62,425 = 40.1, so test time falls about 40 times even though 20 % more patterns are needed.
Data ratio. 20,000,000 ÷ 480,000 = 41.7: the tester memory needed for stimulus falls about 42 times; responses fall similarly through the compactor.
Why it works. Most bits of an ATPG vector are don't-cares; only a few per cent are specified, so a small stream of tester bits can be expanded into the full vector by a linear decompressor.
Costs. Area for the decompressor and compactor; more patterns because some vectors cannot be encoded; unknown (X) values in responses must be masked before the compactor; and diagnosis is harder.
Check. Both designs load the same 10,000 cells; the compressed one does it in 25 clocks per pattern instead of 1,250, a ratio of 50 per pattern, reduced to 40 overall by the extra patterns.

bank.q: Compare stuck-at testing with delay testing. Why must delay faults be tested at speed? Use a two-input AND gate whose input A is slow to rise, with a 1.2 ns path, a 1.0 ns defect and a 2.0 ns clock.
outline: Numerical case at 2.0 ns and 10 ns
answer: Stuck-at faults are static: a line holds 0 or 1 whatever happens. One vector that activates the fault and propagates it to an output is enough, and the speed of the test does not matter.

Delay faults are about time: the logic value is right but arrives late. A transition fault makes one line slow to rise or fall; a path delay fault makes a whole path too slow even when every gate is only a little slow. Resistive opens, resistive bridges and weak transistors cause them, and they grow in importance as clock periods shrink.

Two-vector test. V1 sets the starting value, the launch edge applies V2 and creates the transition, and the capture edge one clock period later stores the result. If the path is slow, the old value is captured.

answer.text: Numerical case. Z = A·B, A slow to rise. V1 = (A, B) = (0, 1), V2 = (1, 1).

answer: Why at speed. The slow tester waits 10 ns, longer than the faulty 2.2 ns, so the delay is invisible. Only a capture one rated period after launch exposes it. The slack of this path is 2.0 − 1.2 = 0.8 ns, so defects smaller than 0.8 ns escape even at speed; those small delays are caught only through longer paths.

In scan designs the pair is made in two ways. Launch-on-shift: the last shift clock creates V2, then capture follows at speed; easy ATPG but SE must switch fast. Launch-on-capture: V1 is shifted in, a first functional clock launches V2 from the logic itself, a second captures; SE can be slow, but ATPG is harder.

Comparison. Stuck-at test: one vector per fault, small pattern count, no timing needs, high coverage of hard defects. Delay test: two vectors per fault, more patterns, an accurate at-speed clock (often from the on-chip PLL), and path selection for path delay faults. Both are needed: stuck-at for opens and shorts, delay for chips that are logically right but too slow.
Check. The faulty arrival 2.2 ns exceeds the 2.0 ns capture time by 0.2 ns, so the at-speed test captures the old 0; at 10 ns it does not.

bank.q: Evaluate full scan, partial scan and logic BIST for a large SoC built from reused IP cores. Recommend a test strategy.
outline: Requirements of an SoC with cores
Full scan: coverage, ATPG, cost, test time
Logic BIST: field test, aliasing, X-sources, test points
answer: Requirements. High stuck-at and transition coverage for low DPM; test time that fits the tester budget; few pins; cores from vendors that arrive with their own tests; and, for automotive or safety parts, self-test in the field.

Full scan. Every flip-flop is a scan cell, so combinational ATPG reaches very high coverage with modest effort, and failing patterns can be diagnosed. Costs: a multiplexer per flip-flop and a delay on functional paths, SE routing, and long shift times. Example: 10,000 patterns through chains of 1,000 cells at 100 MHz take (1,001 × 10,000 + 1,000) × 10 ns = 100.1 ms per chip. Compression cuts this many times.

Partial scan. Only chosen flip-flops are scanned, usually to break feedback loops. It saves some area and delay on critical paths, but ATPG must handle the remaining sequential logic, run time rises and coverage usually falls. For a large SoC the savings are small compared with the coverage lost, so it suits only timing-critical blocks.

Logic BIST. An LFSR feeds the scan chains and a MISR collects their outputs. It needs no tester memory, can run at speed and in the field, and suits reused cores. Limits: random-pattern-resistant faults need test points or reseeding; any unknown (X) value corrupts the MISR, so X-sources must be blocked; aliasing about 2⁻ⁿ; and area for the generator, analyser and controller. Because BIST is not limited by tester pins, it can use many short chains: 100,000 random patterns through 100-cell chains take (101 × 100,000 + 100) × 10 ns ≈ 0.101 s.

Core access. Whatever the logic test, each core needs an IEEE 1500 wrapper, a TAM sized to its scan chains, and a schedule that fits the power limit. A JTAG port sets all modes and tests the board wiring.

Recommendation. Use full scan with compression on all digital logic for production test, for the highest coverage and good diagnosis. Add logic BIST on the same chains for at-speed and in-field self-test where the product needs it, with test points for resistant faults. Use memory BIST (March C− or stronger) for every embedded memory. Keep partial scan only where a multiplexer cannot fit a critical path. Wrap every core and schedule cores in parallel where their chain counts leave TAM wires idle.
Check. The strategy meets each requirement: coverage and diagnosis from scan, field test from BIST, pins from compression and JTAG, core reuse from wrappers.

bank.q: A 3-bit ADC with a full-scale range of 0.8 V is measured with a ramp histogram. The inner codes 1 to 6 have widths 100, 120, 80, 150, 50 and 100 mV, and the measured SINAD is 18.5 dB. Find DNL, INL and ENOB, and analyse what each measurement tells and how test limits are set.
outline: DNL per code, INL as running sum
Offset and gain errors removed first

answer.text: DNL and INL. DNLk = Wk ÷ 100 mV − 1; INLk = DNL1 + … + DNLk.

answer: What DNL tells. The worst DNL is ±0.5 LSB, at codes 4 and 5. No code has DNL = −1, so there are no missing codes; with |DNL| below 1 LSB the converter is monotonic.
What INL tells. The worst INL is +0.5 LSB, at the edge after code 4: the transfer curve bends half an LSB away from the ideal line there. INL limits accuracy for DC measurements.

Offset and gain. Offset error is the shift of the whole curve and gain error the slope error; both are removed before DNL and INL, which is why the six widths add to 600 mV = 6 LSB exactly and INL ends at 0.

Dynamic tests. SNR leaves harmonics out; SINAD includes noise and distortion. An ideal 3-bit converter has SNR = 6.02 × 3 + 1.76 = 19.82 dB. ENOB = (18.5 − 1.76) ÷ 6.02 = 2.78 bits, so noise and distortion cost about 0.2 bit.

Setting limits. Limits come from the data sheet, for example |DNL| ≤ 0.75 LSB, |INL| ≤ 1 LSB, ENOB ≥ 2.7 bits. The tester's own uncertainty is then subtracted as a guard band: with ±0.1 LSB uncertainty the test limits become 0.65 and 0.9 LSB, so a part that passes the test is sure to meet the specification. Wider guard bands mean fewer escapes but more good parts thrown away (yield loss).
Verdict. Worst DNL 0.5 ≤ 0.65, worst INL 0.5 ≤ 0.9 and ENOB 2.78 ≥ 2.7: the part passes.
Check. The INL column returns to 0 at code 6 because the widths sum to the ideal 600 mV.

bank.q: Discuss the test flow of a chip from wafer to system. Include known-good die, burn-in, in-circuit test, boundary scan, SoC test access and test compression, and evaluate where each catches faults most cheaply.
outline: Wafer sort, package test, board test, system test
Cost per fault rises by level
answer: Wafer sort. A probe card contacts every die: DC checks, scan and memory BIST at modest speed. Bad die are inked or mapped and never packaged.
Package (final) test. The packaged part runs the full program at speed, hot and cold, catching bonding and assembly faults and speed failures that the probe cannot measure.
Burn-in. Hours at raised voltage and temperature turn weak parts (thin oxide, marginal vias) into dead ones, so infant failures happen in the factory; a retest removes them.

Board test. In-circuit test presses a bed of nails onto every net and measures parts; a flying probe does it without a fixture, slowly. On dense boards with ball-grid arrays, boundary scan (EXTEST) checks the nets through four pins.
System test. The product boots and runs its software. It is the only level that tests the whole product, and the most expensive place to find and debug a fault.

answer.text: Why earlier is cheaper. Taking 1000 die, 200 bad, wafer sort at ₹6 per die catching 90 % of the bad ones, and packaging at ₹80:

answer: Known-good die. For multi-chip modules and 3D stacks, die are sold bare; one bad die scraps the module, so wafer-level test must be as thorough as final test, often at speed and with burn-in at wafer level.

SoC access. Cores are wrapped (IEEE 1500) and fed through a TAM; scheduling packs cores by chain count and power. Two cores with 4 chains each on an 8-wire TAM finish in 120,950 clocks side by side instead of 221,650 one after the other.

Compression and test coding. Patterns are written for the tester with timing in a standard format such as STIL, and compression expands a few tester channels into hundreds of short chains, cutting tester time and memory many times.

Evaluation. Logic and memory faults are cheapest to catch at wafer sort with scan and BIST; assembly and speed faults at final test; weak parts through burn-in; solder and wiring faults at board test with boundary scan; interaction and software faults only at system test. A good flow puts each fault class at the earliest level that can see it.
Check. The per-good-die costs agree with the totals: 80,000 ÷ 800 = 100.00 and 71,600 ÷ 800 = 89.50.

glossary.def: A faulty circuit ending with the golden signature, so BIST passes it; about 2⁻ⁿ for an n-bit MISR.
Automatic test equipment: the tester that drives and senses the chip pins.
Automatic test pattern generation: finding input vectors that detect chosen faults.
Built-in logic block observer: a register that can act as a normal register, scan register, LFSR or MISR.
Built-in self-test: on-chip pattern generation and response checking.
Test cells at the pins of a chip, chained so board wiring can be tested through a serial port (IEEE 1149.1).
Running parts for hours at raised voltage and temperature to screen early-life failures.
How easily a node can be set to 0 or 1 from the primary inputs.
Gates with D or D̄ on an input and an unknown output, where the fault effect can move forward.
Fraction of shipped parts that are bad, often given in DPM.
Differential nonlinearity: the error of one ADC code width, in LSB.
Detected faults divided by all faults in the fault list, as a percentage.
Detected faults divided by the faults not proved redundant.
Quiescent supply current; a high value reveals shorts and bridges.
Integral nonlinearity: the running sum of DNL, the distance of a code edge from the ideal line.
A bare die proved good before it is bonded into a module or stack.
Linear feedback shift register; used as a pseudo-random pattern generator.
A memory test made of elements that visit every address in a set order with fixed reads and writes.
Multiple-input signature register: an LFSR that compresses many outputs into one signature.
How easily the value of a node can be seen at a primary output.
A fault no input vector can detect, because the logic it sits in is redundant.
Scan flip-flops joined into a shift register from scan-in to scan-out.
A line that always reads 0 (SA0) or always reads 1 (SA1).
Test access mechanism: on-chip wires that carry test data to core wrappers.
Test access port: TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO (and optional TRST) with its 16-state controller.
A line that is slow to rise or slow to fall.
The fraction of die on a wafer that are good.
